Ladder

How many times a fact must come back before it counts as known.

Run length

Mnemonics alone don't produce mastery — they're hooks. Retrieval under difficulty is what actually builds the memory. Use the tricks to get a fact in, use the drill to keep it.

The protocol

One block per sitting. Same five moves every time.

  1. Blind dump first

    Before you open the block's pages, write everything you already know about that topic on a blank sheet. Two minutes, no peeking. This feels bad and is the single highest-yield thing on this list — it tells you exactly where the holes are and makes the reading that follows stick harder.

  2. Read once, fill the blanks

    Your notes are already cloze-formatted — every _______ is a retrieval prompt. Cover the handwritten answer, say it out loud, then check. Don't highlight. Highlighting feels like learning and isn't.

  3. Build the table yourself

    For any topic with a table (isoenzymes, cardiac markers, Fredrickson types, thyroid patterns), redraw the table from memory with the headers filled and the cells empty. Fill it in. Compare. The cells you missed become your error log.

  4. Drill the block

    Open the Drill tab, filter to that topic, run it to zero. Cards you miss come back the next day; cards you hit slide out to 2, 4, 8, then 16 days.

  5. Interleave the day after

    Next sitting, run Drill on All topics for ten minutes before starting the new block. Mixing topics is harder and that's the point — the board doesn't ask questions in chapter order.

Two rules that decide everything

Never re-read to "review"

Re-reading produces fluency, not memory. If you want to review a block you've already done, drill it or blind-dump it. Open the notes only to check an answer.

Keep a one-page error log

Every fact you get wrong twice goes on one sheet of paper. Nothing else. By week four that sheet is your actual syllabus, and it's usually about forty items — not eight hundred.

The 14 blocks

Tick them off. Saved on this device. Blocks marked heavy need two sittings.

Fitting it to your calendar

Six weeks or more: one block per day, five days a week. Day six is a pure drill day across all topics. Day seven off — sleep consolidates this, skipping rest costs you more than the hours gain.

Three weeks: two blocks a day, alternate reading-heavy blocks with number-heavy ones so you're not doing two memorisation slogs back to back.

One week: drop steps 1 and 3, run Drill on everything twice a day, and live in the Numbers and Traps tabs. This is triage, not mastery — say so to yourself honestly so you know what you're trading.

Studying on another laptop

Progress is saved inside this browser only. To carry it over, save a progress file here, copy it to the other laptop (USB, email, OneDrive), and load it there. Loading merges: for every fact it keeps whichever laptop got further, so nothing is lost if you studied on both. Covers every subject, including your ParaDex and BactaDex.

Two skills the flashcards can't touch: running a calculation on numbers you've never seen, and producing a whole table from an empty grid. Both are what the exam actually asks for.

Calculations

Fresh numbers every time. Type the answer, no rounding needed — anything within half a percent counts.

Where each formula comes from

Every one of these is derivable. If you know why the constant is there, you can rebuild the formula when your memory of it goes blank mid-exam.

Build the table

Headers given, cells empty. Fill what you can, then check. Spelling is graded loosely; the fact is what matters.
